seasons.review_body: The original BBC series Criminal Justice was a clinical examination of how ordinary people get chewed up by a system that processes guilt as a bureaucratic convenience. The Indian adaptation, directed by Tigmanshu Dhulia, makes one central addition: Madhav Mishra, played by Pankaj Tripathi as a man whose competence is perennial and whose ethics are situational. The first season follows Aditya Sharma (Vikrant Massey), a young man who wakes up next to a murdered woman with no memory of the night and no resources to fight the system now arresting him for it. The show is at its best in the procedural mechanics - the Bombay court system's rhythms, the negotiation of bail, the theatre of cross-examination - and Tripathi turns Mishra's dry wit into a kind of moral armour that the show is quietly suspicious of. Jackie Shroff as the antagonist and Mita Vashisht as the prosecutor are both exceptional. The season established a franchise; the character of Mishra became appointment television.

episode_reviews.title: The Night It Began
episode_reviews.review_body:
# Criminal Justice S1E1: "The Night It Began" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The call comes from Bandra West: an accident, and something upstairs. Within minutes, the episode has moved past arguments, protocols, compensation, and a promised trip to Kashmir. The police identify **Roshni Saluja**, 31. The apparent cause of death is a slit throat. A home becomes a crime scene. A husband loses control of the story he was trying to manage. A wife asks for essentials while the house is sealed. BollyAI's read: "The Night It Began" is strongest when it lets procedure crush domestic performance, one order at a time.

## The Law Arrives Before the Body

The premiere begins away from murder. It begins with law as argument. **Ratna** is told that IPC Section 323 applies to voluntarily causing physical injury, and a lawyer urges compensation as the cleaner option because a case could drag for five to ten years. That opening matters. The justice system first appears as negotiation, delay, pressure, paperwork. Here, law enters as a room full of people calculating damage.

That frame gives the later murder investigation a harder edge. When the hour moves to Bandra West, the same system changes temperature. No one is talking about accepting money to avoid years of litigation. The language becomes orders, forensics, next-of-kin notification, interrogation, search. The premiere’s argument sits in that shift: criminal justice stays elastic until a body appears, then it turns rigid.

The early dialogue-heavy stretch risks dryness. The legal and protocol talk carries useful information, but it also asks for patience before the episode has given viewers a character to hold onto. Still, the stiffness has a purpose. The show is building a world where institutions speak in sections, affidavits, and process long before anyone says the word that will end the hour.

## A Birthday Promise With Snow on It

The Kashmir promise is the episode’s cleanest piece of emotional misdirection. A father promises his daughter a daddy-daughter trip to see snow. It is a soft, ordinary beat, the kind that could feel disposable until the episode traps the family inside police procedure. Once the house is sealed, that promise feels like a private life interrupted mid-sentence.

The family-celebration banter also changes the rhythm. After the legal opening, the hour briefly lets itself breathe. That tonal pivot matters because the murder plot needs a normal surface to break. Without the birthday texture, the crime-scene response would be efficient but thin. With it, the police arrival feels like an invasion of routine.

**Ira** is described through reports as having hypoglycaemia, and that detail keeps the family material specific. The child has needs that matter in the middle of a police response. That pays off through **Anju Nagpal**, who asks for essential items despite the house being sealed. The beat is small and well judged. Anju is trying to keep a child supported while the machinery around her locks doors.

## Raj Loses the Room

The episode’s central pressure point is **Raj Nagpal** trying to keep access to the life already slipping away from him. Once his affair is surfaced, he wants control of the narrative and movement inside the space. The police response denies both. That is where the premiere finds its bite.

Raj’s contradiction works because it is simple. He wants to keep going, to maintain domestic and private access, to behave as if he can still manage the room. The case says no. The house is sealed. The scene is searched. He is escorted to the station for interrogation after Anju calls the police and the death is treated as murder. Control leaves him in stages, and the episode lets each stage land through procedure rather than speeches.

This compressed second half is stronger. Once the police call begins, the hour stops circling and starts tightening. The visible silence in the investigation beats gives the procedural directives more force. Orders arrive after stillness. The show understands that a crime scene is also a social scene stripped of politeness. People who had roles a few minutes earlier become witnesses, suspects, relatives, officers. Raj cannot charm or explain his way past that new grammar.

## Gauri Turns Panic Into Process

**API Gauri Karmarkar** is the stabilising force of the back half. Her function is not flashy, but it is essential. She wants the case processed methodically, and the episode gives her concrete work: forensics, next-of-kin notification, interrogation, crime-scene search. That sequence could have played like checklist writing. Instead, it becomes the hour’s spine.

Gauri’s presence sharpens the contrast between domestic panic and institutional sequence. Anju needs essentials. Raj needs access. Someone describes failing to save Roshni and hearing Kamala scream. The police need the room treated as evidence. No forced entry is reported, yet the scene appears wiped, and that contradiction plants the episode’s cleanest open loop. If the place was wiped, who had the time and access? If there was no forced entry, what does that say about the person who entered, stayed, or was already inside?

The premiere does not overplay that mystery. It plants it and moves. First episodes often underline every question with ominous music and repeated dialogue. Here, the better tension comes from practical uncertainty: where is the murder weapon, what exactly happened between Raj and Roshni on Ira’s birthday night, and why does the scene appear cleaned if entry was not forced? These are plot questions with procedural weight.

## The Final Word Is a Trapdoor

The ending works because it reduces the whole hour to one domestic sentence: Anju tells someone her husband has been taken in by police for questioning on murder charges. The show has travelled from Section 323 to murder, from compensation talk to a slit throat, from a Kashmir promise to an interrogation room. That movement is the episode’s design.

Where the premiere stumbles is in the early distribution of attention. The legal-protocol opening is thematically useful, but it delays the emotional hook. The hospital material, including the surgeon ordering the new person out for not knowing basic instruments and the hypoglycaemia report, adds institutional texture, yet the connection to the later crime-night pressure is cleaner in idea than in momentum. The episode becomes more confident when the police case takes over.

Still, as a first chapter, "The Night It Began" does the required work with discipline. It introduces law as bargaining, family as performance, and investigation as the force that strips performance away. The murder is the headline, but the craft lies in watching everyday control fail under official process.

## The Verdict

"The Night It Began" is a solid, purposeful opener that improves as it narrows its focus. The first stretch is heavy with legal and protocol talk, and some of that material moves more like scaffolding than drama. Once the Bandra West call arrives, the episode finds its shape: a home becomes evidence, Raj becomes a man under interrogation, and Anju’s practical concern for her daughter cuts through the police seal with human urgency. API Gauri Karmarkar’s methodical case handling gives the back half its grip. BollyAI's read: the premiere earns a 7.2 because its procedural compression is stronger than its setup, but the setup plants enough legal and domestic pressure to make the season’s central trap feel loaded.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere drops Aditya Sharma into a situation so ordinary in its origins and so catastrophic in its consequences that the viewer's discomfort is the point. Massey plays the bewilderment with complete conviction. Tripathi appears late in the episode, but the moment Madhav Mishra walks into the police station, the show's register shifts - you understand immediately what kind of show this is going to be.

critic_note.text: Vikrant Massey anchors the premiere with the precise vulnerability the story demands.

verdict.one_liner: A talky opener finds its bite when domestic control collapses into police procedure and a sealed crime scene.

episode_reviews.title: The Verdict
episode_reviews.review_body: Criminal Justice's season finale delivers its court verdict and then asks the harder question: what justice means in a system that processes cases rather than people. The verdict itself is less important than what the finale does with the aftermath - the distance between the legal result and the human cost it represents. The final scene between Mishra and Aditya is the season's best writing, placing two men on different sides of the privilege divide in the same room to reckon with what the system has extracted from each of them. Pankaj Tripathi's closing argument scene - identified by the Times of India as the moment where the finale delivered on the season's considerable promise - is unusual for a legal drama in that the power of the argument is not the legal points but the human ones. The series went on to a second season with a different case and confirmed the format's viability in the Indian streaming context.

bollymeter.basis: Behind Closed Doors swapped Massey for Kirti Kulhari as the new accused; critics found the case (domestic violence) more emotionally complex but the season slightly less urgent than the first. Tripathi's Mishra remained the anchor.

seasons.review_body: Behind Closed Doors brings a new accused, a new crime, and a significantly more difficult moral case: a domestic violence situation where the law's categories struggle to contain the actual lived reality. Kirti Kulhari is strong; Pankaj Tripathi's Mishra finds new dimensions when defending someone whose guilt is not simply legal. The season's tonal ambition stands out, though the execution can feel rushed across seven episodes.
seasons.season_over_season: New case, new accused, same Mishra - the show's formula holds but the urgency of season 1 is not fully replicated.

bollymeter.basis: Adhura Sach received measured praise - the formula remained reliable, the cases compelling, but the show was settling into a comfort zone. Tripathi's consistency was noted as both the franchise's strength and its limitation.

seasons.review_body: Adhura Sach continued the franchise's reliable procedural formula while circling a media-trial-era case about truth, conviction and the performance of innocence. The show still works, Tripathi is still excellent, and the cases are still more morally complex than most Indian legal drama. The novelty, however, had fully worn off by the third iteration.
seasons.season_over_season: The franchise finds its cruising altitude - dependable rather than surprising.

bollymeter.basis: Season 4 was one of the platform's most-watched Indian originals of 2025. Critics called it the franchise's best work since season 1 - the family-law case gave Tripathi's Mishra more personal stakes than the prior two seasons, and the writing returned to the season 1 quality of moral ambiguity.

pull_quotes.text: Pankaj Tripathi is the most 'khaas aam aadmi' - Criminal Justice season 4 is Waah Vakeel Sahab territory.

seasons.review_body: A Family Matter brought Criminal Justice back to urgency after two seasons of formula maintenance. The family-law case - which critics declined to detail in their reviews to preserve the viewing experience - gives Madhav Mishra stakes that feel genuinely personal rather than professionally convenient. Tripathi delivers his finest work in the franchise since season 1. The Times of India noted the show's 'gripping courtroom drama and strong storytelling'; its strong streaming run confirmed that the audience agreed.
seasons.season_over_season: The franchise's strongest work since season 1 - personal stakes returned, formula discarded.
